articles.title: FDA suspends licences of Mumbai's iconic Cafe Mondegar, 3 other outlets over safety violations
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Tuesday suspended the licences of Cafe Mondegar, a popular restaurant in Colaba, and thr.
articles.body: MUMBAI: The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Tuesday suspended the licences of Cafe Mondegar, a popular restaurant in Colaba, and three other food establishments in Mumbai after inspections found serious food safety and hygiene violations.The FDA inspected Cafe Mondegar at Metro House in Colaba on September 12 and found several deficiencies, including failure to maintain hot food above the prescribed 60 degrees Celsius and cold storage below 5 degrees Celsius, the regulator said in a release.Officials also found improper thawing of food, inadequate rapid cooling of cooked food, and sanitation and structural deficiencies that posed a risk of cross-contamination.The FDA also suspended the licences of Maharashtra Biryani Centre in Kandivali East, Tribhuvan Dairy Farm in Ghatkopar West and Mahavir Cashew & Foods Pvt Ltd in Ghatkopar East after inspections found violations of Schedule 4 of the Food Safety and Standards Act.Schedule 4 lays down mandatory hygiene and sanitation requirements for food business operators.The FDA, under new commissioner Tukaram Mundhe, has intensified its crackdown on food safety, adulteration and hygiene violations. It also took action against nine food establishments in Mumbai for deficiencies found during inspections conducted as part of its festival season drive.The establishments include Ruhafza Bakery in Khar West; Chandru's Pure Ghee Sweets and Sharma Dairy & Fast Food in Andheri West; Punjabi Chandu Halwai LLP at Grant Road East; Shri Narayan Dairy in Vile Parle West; and Gulshan Dairy Farm in Khar West.The regulator said it inspected 38 food establishments in Mumbai and collected 47 food samples, including milk, khoya, ghee and sweets, for analysis during the special festival campaign between September 11 and 14.At Ayush Milk Supplier in Andheri East, officials collected a sample of sweet barfi and seized the remaining 23 kg stock, valued at Rs 6,440. At Brijwasi Mithaiyan Shop in Mulund West, they collected a khoya sample and seized 225 kg of the remaining stock, valued at Rs 60,300.The FDA also took action against several milk and milk-product establishments across Maharashtra.At Shivaratna Milk & Milk Agro Product in Takawade, Kolhapur, officials found 10 kg of halwa worth Rs 6,000 and 198 kg of rabadi worth Rs 45,540, both suspected to be substandard.At Creamy Delight in Patas, Pune, officials found 1,519 kg of cow milk, butter and skimmed milk powder worth Rs 8.50 lakh with labelling deficiencies and suspected substandard quality.At Mahaveer Dairy in Manchar, Pune, officials found 49 kg of khoya worth Rs 13,720, 104 kg of paneer worth Rs 31,200 and 11 kg of ghee worth Rs 7,920, all suspected to be substandard. The FDA said it was initiating further legal action in these cases.In Jalgaon district, the food regulator seized around 2,155 kg of suspected adulterated sweet halwa worth Rs 5.58 lakh from two transport vehicles.It also seized 28 kg of suspected substandard khoya worth Rs 12,600 from Brijvilas Dairy in Jalgaon, 16.2 kg of suspected substandard peda and buffalo ghee worth Rs 15,200 from Ekta Dudh Dairy and Sweets in Raver, and 6.5 kg of peda worth Rs 2,600 from Tarachand Sundarji and Sons in Chalisgaon in Jalgaon district.Officials also found 19 kg of shrikhand worth Rs 5,320 stored in unhygienic conditions at a premises belonging to Samadhan Pawar, the release said.The FDA said it found 30 litres of loose pasteurised standardised buffalo milk, valued at Rs 2,830, being sold at Bhairavnath Dairy in Badlapur, Thane, in violation of an order dated July 3, 2026.At Ayush Milk Supplier in Andheri East, officials also found improper storage and inadequate or incorrect labelling of sweet barfi and low-fat paneer.The regulator said its statewide action resulted in the seizure of 30 litres of liquid milk and 4,138.7 kg of milk products and sweets, including khoya, paneer, ghee, peda, halwa, shrikhand, butter and milk powder. The total value of the seized stock was Rs 15,58,072.In its action against banned food products, the FDA said a joint team of its officials and police seized gutkha and other prohibited food products worth Rs 95.30 lakh in Rajur, Jalna district, on September 9.The team also seized vehicles allegedly used to transport the banned products, valued at around Rs 40 lakh, taking the total value of the seized goods and vehicles to Rs 1.35 crore.Police registered a case against two individuals, Sandeep Dattu Bhumkar and Ashish Dholtani, and the supplier companies under various provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Food Safety and Standards Act, and MCOCA (Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act).In Beed district, a joint FDA-police team intercepted a Mahindra Scorpio allegedly being used to transport banned gutkha near the Barshi Naka area. Officials detained two men, Dattatray Ghodke and Omkar Ghodke, and seized gutkha worth Rs 3.63 lakh and the vehicle worth Rs 7 lakh.A case was registered against the two men and the supplier company under MCOCA, the release said.The FDA further said that in a special drive in Mumbai on September 12, it acted against five establishments where prohibited food products were found.It seized banned food stock worth Rs 20,21,100, registered one FIR and arrested nine people. The regulator also seized five vehicles allegedly used to transport the prohibited products, with their combined value at Rs 98 lakh.(With Agency Inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Nick Reiner will not face death penalty if convicted of killing parents, prosecutors say
articles.summary: Nick Reiner is accused of murdering his parents, Hollywood director Rob Reiner and his wife Michele Reiner.
articles.body:
Prosecutors will not seek the death penalty against Nick Reiner, who is accused of murdering his parents, Hollywood director Rob Reiner and his wife Michele Reiner.

Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman said prosecutors made the decision after "a rigorous review" and wishes of the Reiners' loved ones.

"We did speak with Nick Reiner's siblings (and) they made their views very clear," Hochman told reporters ahead of a pretrial hearing on Wednesday.

Prosecutors said this meant the maximum punishment Nick Reiner will face is life in prison without the possibility of parole, if convicted.

Hochman also said on Tuesday that the trial would not begin until next year.

Rob and Michele Reiner were found stabbed to death in their Los Angeles home last year. Their bodies were reportedly discovered by their daughter Romy on 14 December.

The couple died from "multiple sharp force injuries", the LA County medical examiner said at the time.

Prosecutors allege that Nick Reiner, the couples' youngest son, fatally stabbed his father and mother inside a bedroom of their home before fleeing. He was arrested in Los Angeles the same day.

The 33-year-old faces two counts of first-degree murder, with a special circumstance alleging multiple murders. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Rob Reiner, 78, directed films including This Is Spinal Tap, the Princess Bride, When Harry Met Sally and Stand By Me.

Michele Singer Reiner, 70, was an actress, photographer and producer, and the founder of Reiner Light, a photography agency and production company.

It is unclear if Nick Reiner will appear in court on Tuesday for a hearing about unsealing transcripts from the grand jury that returned the indictment against him.

Reiner's siblings, Jake and Romy, have asked for the transcripts to remain sealed because "the disclosure to the public and media of the details and evidence of the killing of their parents will cause them additional trauma and harm", Hochman said.

articles.title: Qatar warns closure of Bab al-Mandab Strait would be 'catastrophic'
articles.summary: The Gulf state of Qatar said a de facto closure of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which separates Yemen and the Horn of Africa, would be a disaster. "The world is...
articles.body:
Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen have threatened Israeli and US vessels in the Indian Ocean, potentially impacting global maritime trade.

Qatar warns that a de facto closure of the Bab al-Mandab Strait due to Houthi militia control would have catastrophic consequences for international sea routes.

Saudi Arabia is rerouting some of its oil shipments through the Red Sea due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, with concerns about freedom of navigation in the region.

The Gulf state of Qatar said a de facto closure of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which separates Yemen and the Horn of Africa, would be a disaster.

"The world is suffering enough because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz," a spokesman for the Qatari Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday. It could not afford for the sea route through Bab al-Mandab to become impassable as well, he said.

"It would be catastrophic for the whole world."

He added that a blockade of international sea routes could not be allowed to become the "new normal."

The Iran-backed Houthi militia advanced south along the coast of Yemen last week and now controls the coastal towns of Mokha, Dhubab and several islands in the Red Sea. From there, the militia is in a position to attack merchant ships even more effectively than before.

The Bab al-Mandab, or Gate of Tears, connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and lies on the shortest shipping route between Europe and Asia. In normal times, around 10% of global maritime trade and 30% of global container traffic passes through the Strait.

Traffic through the strait fell significantly after the militia started to attack ships in 2023. Many shipping companies opted for the long and expensive detour via the Cape of Good Hope off the coast of South Africa.

Saudi Arabia, the world's leading oil exporter, is attempting to ship some of its oil via the Red Sea, as it has to be rerouted due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman also discussed the matter with Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi during a visit to Cairo on Tuesday.

Egyptian sources said both leaders agreed that freedom of navigation must not be threatened. Like Saudi Arabia, Egypt has a long coastline on the Red Sea.

articles.title: Guernsey band records song that lasts less than a second
articles.summary: A Guernsey band believe their newly released tune is unofficially the shortest song in the world.
articles.body:
A Guernsey band believe their newly released tune Don't let the fire go out, which is under a second long, could be the shortest song in the world.

Coastal Fire Department have made an unofficial attempt to beat the world record set by Napalm Deaths' You Suffer, which was 1.316 seconds long.

Band member Ollie Goddard said he contacted Guinness World Records and was but told the category had been closed after it had been "inundated by requests".

He said the song was "just a bit of fun" and despite being less than a second long still contained lyrics, a cord change, and all three band members.

Goddard said the band were writing and recording their album, with a lot of the songs coming in at about 01:20 and 01:40 in length.

"We knew there was an official world record and we thought can we go under a second - that's what we have done for a bit of a laugh.

"It's unofficially the shortest song... certainly the shortest song ever released on the Channel Islands."

He said any proceeds made from the track would go to the animal charity, The Guernsey Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.

Goddard said he wrote the song two years ago and had sat on it ever since.

He hoped the song would be a reminder to everyone that "If you have hobbies, don't let the fire go out for that".

"Keep doing those things that make you happy," said Goddard.

"It's good to have fun, if we've contributed in anyone having a smile, we have done our job."

articles.title: In 2011, New York covered five acres of Lake George with more than 700 mats to suffocate invasive Asian clams; 97% died, but the invader later spread to 27 locations
articles.summary: US News: When invasive Asian clams were discovered in Lake George, New York, in 2010, researchers moved quickly to test whether covering the lakebed could stop.
articles.body: When invasive Asian clams were discovered in Lake George, New York, in 2010, researchers moved quickly to test whether covering the lakebed could stop the species from spreading. According to a final report by the Darrin Fresh Water Institute at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, published through the Lake Champlain Basin Program, a large-scale treatment was carried out in 2011 across five acres of infested lake bottom using benthic barrier mats. The treatment killed 97% of the Asian clams found in the treated area. But the result did not permanently eliminate the invasive species; subsequent surveys found Asian clams at 27 locations across Lake George, highlighting the difficulty of controlling an invasive species once it becomes established.How the Asian clam arrived in Lake GeorgeThe Asian clam, scientifically known as Corbicula fluminea, was first discovered in Lake George in August 2010. Researchers initially documented densities of as many as 600 clams per square metre across an area of roughly 2.5 acres. The species is a small freshwater bivalve that can reproduce without a mate, allowing even a small number of individuals to establish a population.Asian clams prefer shallow, sandy or gravelly areas, which made parts of Lake George suitable for colonisation. The species can also occur in dense populations, raising concerns about its potential effects on water quality and native aquatic organisms. The discovery prompted the creation of the Lake George Asian Clam Rapid Response Task Force, bringing together organisations including the Lake George Association, Darrin Fresh Water Institute, Lake George Park Commission, New York State Department of Environmental Conservation and Lake Champlain Basin Program. The group began examining whether the newly detected population could still be controlled or eradicated.The plan: cover the lakebed and cut off oxygenOne of the approaches tested was the use of benthic barriers. These are large mats placed directly over the lake bottom to isolate the clams from the surrounding water. The method was intended to reduce oxygen beneath the barriers and eventually suffocate the organisms. In 2011, the treatment expanded across five acres of the southern Lake George basin, between Pine Point and the English Brook Delta. More than 700 mats were placed over the affected lakebed. The mats were essentially heavy plastic barriers that had to remain in close contact with the bottom to prevent the clams from surviving underneath them.The treatment required considerable underwater maintenance. Waves and boat traffic shifted some of the mats, requiring divers to reposition and secure them. Lake Champlain Maritime Museum described how divers also had to “burp” the barriers by releasing gas that accumulated underneath them as organic material decomposed. Keeping the mats flat helped maintain the conditions needed for the treatment to work. Researchers also installed ports in more than 150 mats so divers could collect water samples from underneath the barriers. Those samples were analysed for dissolved oxygen and ammonia each week, allowing the treatment team to track changing conditions beneath the mats and use the results to guide maintenance.97% of the clams were killedThe initial results appeared highly encouraging. After the spring 2011 treatment, mortality surveys found that 97% of the Asian clams in the treated area had died. The experiment demonstrated that benthic barriers could be highly effective at sharply reducing an established population when the affected area could be isolated and covered.But killing most of the clams in one area did not mean the species had been eliminated from Lake George. Later monitoring showed why. The Lake George Association’s surveys found that treated sites could become repopulated after initially successful treatments. According to the organisation’s lakewide survey reporting, microscopic and buoyant juvenile clams outside treated areas could move into previously cleared locations. Even sites where no clams were detected the year after treatment could contain small populations again the following year.From one infestation to 27 locationsThe problem gradually became much larger than the original infestation. A 2019 lakewide survey identified three additional Asian clam sites, bringing the total number of known locations to 27 across Lake George. Most were concentrated in the southern basin, particularly along the more developed western shoreline where sandy habitat is available. The spread demonstrated one of the central challenges of invasive-species control: a treatment can be extremely effective within a defined area while still failing to prevent recolonisation from populations elsewhere in the same waterbody.Lake George's experience also showed why eradication becomes increasingly difficult and expensive as an invasive species expands. The lakewide survey reported that barrier treatments generally produced 96% to 100% mortality at treated sites, but populations often rebounded when even a small number of clams survived or when clams moved back into treated areas. By 2016, the task force halted barrier treatments after concluding that continued lakewide control was not a practical solution with the methods then available.What the Lake George experiment revealedThe Asian clam response in Lake George became an example of both the potential and limitations of rapid invasive-species control. Covering five acres with more than 700 benthic mats produced a striking short-term result, killing 97% of the clams in the treated area. But the species' ability to reproduce rapidly and recolonise treated sites meant that the treatment could not deliver permanent eradication across the lake.Today, Lake George continues to be monitored through lakewide surveys. The focus has shifted from attempting to eliminate every population with benthic barriers towards understanding the species, tracking its distribution and assessing its potential effects on the lake. The experience also underscores why early detection and preventing the movement of aquatic invasive species remain important parts of protecting freshwater ecosystems.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
